questions.prompt: What does the SDProp process do, and how often does it run by default?
options: It replicates GPOs to all DCs every 15 minutes
It stamps the AdminSDHolder object's ACL onto every protected object, running on the PDC Emulator every 60 minutes by default
It resets all user passwords every 24 hours
It backs up the directory database hourly
questions.explanation: SDProp exists to keep privileged objects' permissions consistent with the AdminSDHolder template, overwriting whatever ACL is currently on them, by default once an hour.

questions.prompt: Why does modifying the AdminSDHolder ACL create a self-healing backdoor?
options: Because it disables all auditing on privileged groups
Because SDProp propagates the modified template ACL onto every protected object within the hour, restoring the attacker's permission even after a defender removes it
Because it prevents Domain Admins from logging in
Because AdminSDHolder cannot be modified once set
questions.explanation: The attacker backdoors the template rather than an individual object. Removing the rogue permission from a privileged group without cleaning AdminSDHolder means SDProp restores it on the next cycle.

questions.prompt: A permission you removed from Domain Admins reappears about an hour later. What should you check before concluding the attacker still has live access?
options: The AdminSDHolder object's ACL, since SDProp restoring the template is the more likely explanation
questions.explanation: The roughly-one-hour reappearance interval matches SDProp's default cycle. Checking AdminSDHolder distinguishes a template backdoor from an attacker actively re-adding the permission.

questions.prompt: Why is adminCount = 1 on an account with no current privileged membership worth investigating?
options: adminCount is not automatically reset when an object leaves the protected set, so it is a historical record that the account was privileged at some point
It means the account is currently a Domain Admin
It indicates the account has never been used
questions.explanation: Because the attribute persists after an object leaves the protected set, it forms a trail of past privilege -- sometimes stale administrative leftovers, sometimes an attacker's earlier foothold.
